sre-definicao.name: What SRE is and the 50% rule
sre-definicao.summary: SRE is the discipline that applies software engineering to operations, covering the entire lifecycle; limit of 50% ops work.
rules: Entire lifecycle: from conception to decommissioning (SRE p.15)
Cap of 50% of aggregate time on ops (tickets, on-call, manual work); the excess goes back to development (SRE p.23-24)
Team composition: 50-60% SWE and 40-50% near-SWE with UNIX/networking (SRE p.23) [DATED]
SRE is seen as a specific implementation of DevOps, with extensions (SRE p.24)
not_in_book: SRE and DevOps are the same thing

error-budget.name: Error budget
error-budget.summary: Budget = 1 - availability target; resolves the dev x SRE tension; when exhausted, releases stop.
rules: Error budget = 1 - availability target (SRE p.25; p.330)
Measured by a neutral third party (monitoring), quarterly period in Ch. 3 (SRE p.42-43) and 'often a month' in App. B (SRE p.330)
When exhausted: temporarily suspend releases and invest in testing/resilience (SRE p.43)
Requires the SRE to have the authority to stop launches (SRE p.43)
Example: 99.999% -> 0.001%; a 0.0002% failure consumes 20% (SRE p.43)

sli-slo-sla.name: SLI, SLO and SLA
sli-slo-sla.summary: The indicator measures, the objective sets the target, the agreement carries consequences.
rules: An SLI is a quantitative measure (latency, error rate, throughput) (SRE p.44)
An SLO is a target or range for an SLI (SRE p.45)
An SLA has consequences; test: 'what happens if the SLO is not met?' (SRE p.45)

SRE normally does not build SLAs (business/product decision, SRE p.45); business and legal choose the consequences and the SRE helps assess the likelihood/difficulty of meeting the SLOs (SRE p.49); note 16: 'SLA' often means SLO, and an actual SLA violation can become a contractual dispute (SRE p.50)
Prefer percentiles to averages (SRE p.47)
Do not choose the target by current performance; few SLOs; no absolutes; perfection can wait (SRE p.48-49)
Internal SLO tighter than the published one; do not overperform the SLO by much (SRE p.49)
Latency SLO examples: 99% of Gets in < 100 ms; 90% < 1 ms and 99% < 10 ms; 99.9% < 100 ms (SRE p.48); typical = 50 ms with 5% 20x slower (SRE p.47)

disponibilidade.name: Availability, nines and the downtime table
disponibilidade.summary: By time: uptime/(uptime+downtime); aggregate: successes/total; Appendix A table.
rules: Availability by time = uptime/(uptime+downtime) (SRE p.38)
Aggregate = successful requests/total requests over a moving window (SRE p.38)
99.99% = 52.56 min/year; 2.5M req/day at 99.99% = 250 errors (SRE p.38)
Appendix A table in 6 periods, 8 levels (SRE p.326-327)
Published Google Compute Engine target: 'three and a half nines' = 99.95% (SRE p.44); Apps for Work: external quarterly target of 99.9% (SRE p.39)

toil.name: Toil
toil.summary: Manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical work with no enduring value, O(n); target below 50%.
rules: Six attributes: manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, no enduring value, O(n) (SRE p.51-52)
Overhead (meetings, HR) and 'grungy' work with enduring value are not toil (SRE p.51)
Target: toil < 50% of time; floor per rotation: 2/6 = 33%, 2/8 = 25% (SRE p.52)
In excess it causes stagnation, low morale, friction, broken promises (SRE p.53)

Note 21: 'it is not toil because it requires human judgment' calls for care: does the task really require judgment or is that a design flaw? (e.g. a service that alerts several times a day with complex responses) (SRE p.53)

automacao.name: Automation
automacao.summary: Automation as a force multiplier; hierarchy of 5 classes; Decider, Prodtest and Diskerase cases.
rules: Values: consistency, platform, faster repairs and actions, time savings (SRE p.63-64)
Five classes, from 'no automation' to 'a system that needs no automation' (SRE p.66)
Decider: MySQL failover in <30 s in 95% of cases (SRE p.66-67)
Diskerase: empty set interpreted as 'all'; sanity checks, rate limiting, idempotence (SRE p.74)
Decider: Ads MySQL failover < 30 s in 95% (SRE p.67); Diskerase: empty set = everything (SRE p.74); see decider-ads-mysql and prodtest-turnup

Automation as meta-software: uses (accounts, turnup and turndown, rollouts, runtime configuration); SRE focus on the lifecycle of systems, not on data; high-level abstractions leak (a binary push is not atomic); prefer building platforms (SRE p.65)

Maximalist view (p.65): it is not appropriate to automate every component of every system; not everyone has the capacity or inclination to develop automation at every moment; essential systems were born as prototypes not designed for automation; Google chose to build platforms (SRE p.65)

Rare automation and bit rot (p.66): turnup automation kept outside the system suffers bit rot; couple the failure through misaligned priorities (devs resist test deploys on every change); rarely executed automation is hard to test and fragile; classic example: cluster failover every few months (SRE p.66)
not_in_book: quantitative rule for when to automate

monitoramento.name: Monitoring and golden signals
monitoramento.summary: Four signals, white/black-box, symptom vs cause, three outputs (page, ticket, log).
rules: Four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation (SRE p.57-58)
Alert on symptoms; page only what is actionable and urgent (SRE p.56, 59-60)
Valid outputs: alert, ticket, logging (SRE p.26; p.95; p.330)
Do not rely on averages; use histograms (SRE p.58)
Tail: a 100 ms average at 1,000 req/s can hide 1% taking 5 s; the backend's p99 becomes the frontend's median (SRE p.58)
The term definitions on p.55 (root cause, alert, node, machine, dashboard and others) are in the topic definicoes-cap6-p55 (SRE p.55)
Note 25: zero redundancy (N + 0) and nearly full parts count as imminent saturation (SRE p.62)
Saturation also involves predicting imminent saturation (e.g. the disk fills in 4 hours); note 25 (p.62) says that zero redundancy (N + 0) and nearly full parts count as imminent (SRE p.58, 62)

A collection/alert exercised less than once per quarter by some teams is a candidate for removal; the 1-2 min threshold for probing/disk is on p.59; 'urgent and actionable' on p.59-60, p.56 and the cost of paging (SRE p.56, 59-60)

alertas-series-temporais.name: Alerts from time series (Borgmon)
alertas-series-temporais.summary: Mass collection of /varz, central rule evaluation, Alertmanager; Prometheus has similar principles.
rules: Counters preferred to gauges; rate() over a window (SRE p.92-93)
Alert with a minimum duration to avoid flapping; example 'for 2m' (SRE p.94-95)
Alertmanager inhibits, deduplicates and routes (SRE p.95)
Black-box prober on the frontend and the backend (SRE p.96)
Borgmon: ~24 bytes per point, ~12 h of horizon and < 17 GB for 1 million series (SRE p.90-91); detail in the topic borgmon-dimensionamento
not_in_book: Monarch in detail (only cited in Ch. 31)

release.name: Release engineering
release.summary: Four principles: self-service, high velocity, hermetic builds, enforcement of policies.
rules: Hermetic build: same revision, same result (SRE p.77)
Release branch cut at a revision and never merged back; cherry picks (SRE p.78)
Adjust the deploy to the risk profile (SRE p.80)
Four configuration management models (SRE p.80)

Branch: cut from the mainline at a revision and never merged back; fixes go to the mainline and are cherry-picked into the branch, so as not to pick up by mistake unrelated changes submitted to the mainline after the original build (direction mainline -> branch); this way the exact content of each release is known (SRE p.78)

CI test targets = targets that block the release; create the release at the revision of the last continuous build that passed; rerun the tests on the branch with an audit trail because, with cherry picks, the branch may have a version of the code that does not exist on the mainline (SRE p.78)
MPM: named packages, versioned with a unique hash and signed; labels (dev, canary, production) move automatically; the book does not state the hash algorithm (SRE p.78)

testes.name: Reliability testing
testes.summary: Traditional and production tests; canary; probes; configuration.
rules: Traditional tests: unit, integration, system (smoke, performance, regression) (SRE p.136-137)
Production tests: configuration, stress, canary (SRE p.138-139)
Canary: 0.1% of traffic, orders of magnitude every 24 h (note SRE p.147)
Noisy break-glass and tests not disabled (SRE p.144)
Production probes: known bad, known good replayable and not replayable (SRE p.145)
Canary: start with 0.1% of traffic and increase by orders of magnitude every 24 h (note 89, p.147); with growth from 1% to 10% in 24 h, K ~ 10 h 25 min (note 90)
The 42,000-test calculation: a service with more than 21,000 simple tests (before and after the patch); accepting 99% of perfect patches requires each test to be right > 99.9999% (SRE p.142-143)
Bazel: dependency graph, only the tests of the changed code (SRE p.140, 147 n.93)
Canary of Ch. 17 (0.1% of traffic, note 89, p.147) and canary of Ch. 27 (a few machines of a datacenter, automatic rollback, p.268): see canario-feature-flags
Note 86 (p.147): scheduler and executors (sandbox of the test binaries) form shared test infrastructure; note 98: repeating the seed does not serialize task deaths with the fake traffic (SRE p.147)

Barriers against risky software (3 steps): a barrier in the replication configuration so the replica does not pass the health check; the risky software checks the barrier at startup and only accesses unhealthy replicas; the black-box monitoring validation tool removes the barrier; automation tools have out-of-band risk and circular dependency; DR tools can operate offline with a checkpoint (SRE p.141)
Stability drives agility: a predictably solid build lets developers iterate faster (SRE p.140)

on-call.name: On-call
on-call.summary: Limits on the quantity and quality of on-call.
rules: <=25% of time on-call and >=50% on engineering (SRE p.100)
8 people at one site; 6 per site at two (SRE p.100)
At most 2 incidents per 12 h shift (6 h per incident) (SRE p.101)
Typical response times: 5 min and 30 min (SRE p.99)
Give back the pager in extreme cases (SRE p.102-103)
Target of 1:1 between alerts and incidents; 99.99% in the quarter ~ 13 min of downtime (SRE p.99-102)
Primary and secondary: the secondary can be the fall-through for missed pages or handle non-urgent work; two related teams can be each other's secondary (SRE p.100)
Page distribution should be flat, with a likely median of 0; incidents per day > 1 every day indicates something is going to break (SRE p.101)
Stress (cortisol, CRH) favors heuristics such as confirmation bias; clear escalation, incident procedures and blameless postmortem help (SRE p.101)
Pages should be aligned with the symptoms that threaten the SLO and be actionable; group related alerts, silence duplicates, approach 1:1 alert/incident (SRE p.102)
Give back the pager: the development team is exclusively on call until the system reaches the standard; rare; temporary alternative: route part of the pages to the developers' on-call (SRE p.102-103)

troubleshooting.name: Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.summary: Hypothetico-deductive method; triage; stop the bleeding.
rules: Flow: report, telemetry/logs, hypotheses, tests, cause, fix, postmortem (SRE p.104)
In a serious outage, stop the bleeding before the root cause, preserving evidence (SRE p.106-107)
Ask 'what touched it last' (SRE p.109)
Negative results are conclusive and should be published (SRE p.110-111)
Effective report: expected behavior, actual behavior and, if possible, how to reproduce; open a bug for each problem; discourage reporting directly to a person (SRE p.106)

Test and Treat, five cautions: mutually exclusive alternatives, obvious first, confounding factors, side effects of active tests, tests that are only suggestive; write everything down with timestamps (SRE p.110, 115)
Negative results are magic: negative results are conclusive (example: a web server that sustains ~800 of 8,000 connections) and should be published (SRE p.110-111)
Cure: several factors together can be the cause and systems are path-dependent; a non-production environment helps at the cost of another copy (SRE p.111)

App Engine: latency ~10x, CPU and processes ~4x; 250 ms without RPC (Dapper does not help); mitigated before understanding (instance with more CPU); cause: a whitelist created on each access to a path, thousands of objects in half an hour by a security scanner (SRE p.112-114)
RE2 does not backtrack and grows linearly; PCRE can take exponential time (note 68, p.115); Hickam's dictum (note 62); unique request ID (SRE p.114-115)
Correlation is not causation: packet loss in the cluster and failing disks have a common cause, a power outage (SRE p.106)

incidentes.name: Incident management
incidentes.summary: Incident Command System with 4 roles and a living document.
rules: Roles: Incident Command, Operational Work, Communication, Planning (SRE p.123)
Only Ops modifies the system (SRE p.123)
Declare if it needs a second team, is customer-visible, or goes unsolved after an hour (SRE p.125)
Explicit handoff with confirmation (SRE p.124)
App. C: state document of incident #465 (IC, Ops, Planning, Comms; exit: 99.99% and p99 < 100 ms for 30+ min) (SRE p.332-333)
Unmanaged incident (Mary): three hazards: narrow technical focus, poor communication and freelancing (a deploy without CPU affinity coordination took the servers down) (SRE p.122-123)

Roles: IC keeps the high-level state and in fact holds all the roles not delegated; Ops lead is the only group that modifies the system; Communication issues periodic updates; Planning files bugs, orders dinner, organizes handoffs and tracks the divergence from normal (SRE p.123)
If the load of a role is excessive, ask the planning lead for more people and delegate (including sub-incidents); separating the roles well gives more autonomy (SRE p.123)
Command post: war room or desks with email and IRC; IRC serves as a log and bots record the incident traffic (SRE p.123)
Living document: editable by several people (Google Docs; the Google Docs SRE uses Google Sites), template, important information at the top, kept for the postmortem (SRE p.124)
Handoff: say 'you are now the incident commander, okay?' and only leave the call with a firm acceptance; communicate to everyone (SRE p.124)

Managed incident: handoff to the sister office at 18:00 after a call at 17:45; declare early; the skill atrophies without use: use the framework in operational changes and in DiRT; it reduces MTTR (SRE p.124-125)

postmortem.name: Postmortem
postmortem.summary: Blameless written record; triggers; review; Appendix D template.
rules: Triggers: downtime above the threshold, data loss, on-call intervention, resolution time, monitoring failure (SRE p.126)
Blameless: focus on systemic causes (SRE p.126-127)
Review criteria: 5 questions (SRE p.127)
13 template fields in App. D (SRE p.334-336)
App. D in full (incident #465: 66 min of outage, 89 min of incident, 1.21 billion queries lost): see incidente-shakespeare-ap-d (SRE p.334-336)
Blameless was born in healthcare and aviation; example of finger-pointing vs blameless (rewrite the backend); do not stigmatize those who produce postmortems frequently (SRE p.127)
Review: a group of seniors evaluates with five questions; no postmortem left unreviewed; repository of past incidents (Etsy released Morgue, note 81 printed on p.129) (SRE p.127-129)

Culture: postmortem of the month, discussion group, reading clubs, Wheel of Misfortune; trial period; reward publicly; TGIF 2014: an SRE rolled back in 4 min a release that took down a critical service and received 2 peer bonuses (SRE p.128)
Postmortems at Google: working group with templates, automation and metadata fields for trend analysis (SRE p.129)
App. D notes: 164 (5 Whys), 165 (extreme or expensive reflex actions), 166 (Where we got lucky = near misses), 167 (timeline as a script) (SRE p.336)

Google's Peer Bonus program (note 82, SRE p.129) lets colleagues recognize exceptional effort and involves a symbolic cash reward; the book does not state the amount; 2 peer bonuses at TGIF 2014 (SRE p.128-129)
The template gained additional metadata fields without enumerating them; App. D is an example postmortem, not the list of those fields (SRE p.129)

outalator.name: Outage tracking (Outalator)
outalator.summary: Aggregates alerts into incidents and allows analysis and tags.
rules: Escalator tracks acknowledge and escalates (SRE p.130)
Outalator groups alerts into incidents and keeps annotations (SRE p.130-131)
Hierarchical colon-separated tags; 'bogus' for a false positive (SRE p.131-133)

load-balancing.name: Load balancing
load-balancing.summary: DNS and VIP at the frontend; lame duck, subsetting and WRR in the datacenter.
rules: DNS with low TTL and a 512-byte limit; EDNS0 as a partial solution (SRE p.160-161)
VIP: consistent hashing; GRE with 24 bytes of overhead (SRE p.161-162)
Lame duck allows a clean shutdown; window 10-150 s (SRE p.166)
Subset of 20-100 backends; deterministic subsetting (SRE p.167-170)
Weighted Round Robin beats Round Robin and Least-Loaded (SRE p.172-174)
VIP: Google's current solution = GRE encapsulation (24 B of overhead) (SRE p.162); mod N remaps almost everything (SRE p.161-162)
Round Robin up to 2x CPU spread; Least-Loaded 'as bad as' RR; WRR reduced the spread (SRE p.171, 173-174); see round-robin-least-loaded-wrr

overload.name: Overload and throttling
overload.summary: QPS is a bad metric; per-client quotas; adaptive throttling; criticality; retry budgets.
rules: Measure capacity in CPU, not QPS (SRE p.175-176)
Adaptive throttling: requests vs accepts over 2 min, K=2 (SRE p.176-177)
Criticality: CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS, SHEDDABLE (SRE p.177)
Retries: 3 per request and 10% per client (SRE p.179)
Global overload: it is vital to deliver errors only to the clients that misbehave, leaving the others intact; the owner provisions by the negotiated usage and sets per-client quotas (SRE p.176)
The per-datacenter balancer does not send more than 100 tasks x 500 req/s = 50,000 QPS; the book notes that even this may be insufficient (SRE p.175)
Doorman appears only in note 106 (SRE p.183) as an example of cooperative, distributed client-side throttling; the book describes no algorithm or parameters and does not formally recommend it

Connection load: a large pool and churn cost CPU/memory; health checks from idle clients (TCP becomes UDP) can cost more than serving; mitigate by reducing the frequency or creating/destroying connections dynamically (SRE p.182)
Batch bursts: balance across datacenters by cluster utilization, or a batch proxy (batch client -> batch proxy -> backend) that acts as a fuse and allows larger subsets (SRE p.182)
not_in_book: readable throttling formula (illegible figure in the PDF)
algorithm, token bucket or leases of Doorman (only note 106, p.183)

cascading-failures.name: Cascading failures
cascading-failures.summary: Positive feedback; prevention, testing and mitigation. Deadline rules (propagate the absolute one, reduce the outgoing one by a few hundred ms, ceiling for non-critical backends, cancellation), queues (small in steady traffic; in bursts by threads in use, time per request and size and frequency of bursts), retries, health checks and immediate steps.
rules: Definition and causes: overload, resources, unavailability (SRE p.184, 187-188)

Numeric example: healthy at 10,000 QPS and cascade at 11,000 QPS; dropping to 9,000 QPS almost certainly does not stop the crashes; with 10% of the servers healthy, the load would have to fall to about 1,000 QPS (SRE p.188)
Prevention (rough priority order): load test, degradation, rejection, capacity planning (SRE p.188-189)
Randomized exponential backoff; 4^3 = 64 attempts (SRE p.191-192)
Propagate deadlines and cancellations (SRE p.192-193)
Immediate steps: 7 actions (SRE p.198-199); the order of that list is not declared as a ranking
Drop Traffic: if the whole service is in a crash loop, consider being aggressive and letting only ~1% of the traffic through, then raise it gradually (SRE p.198)
Process health check x service health check; temporarily disabling health checks can stabilize (SRE p.198)
9-step chain (badly tuned GC -> CPU -> RAM -> cache miss -> backend -> health checks) (SRE p.188)
Full incident of App. D (88x, sacrificial cluster, 2x failed, 10x, return in steps): see incidente-shakespeare-ap-d (SRE p.332-336)
Outgoing deadline (p.193): reduce the outgoing deadline slightly (a few hundred ms) to cover network transit and post-processing on the client (SRE p.193)

Ceiling (upper limit) for outgoing deadlines: for non-critical backends or those that usually respond quickly; understand the traffic mix so as not to make certain kinds of request (large payload, heavy computation) always fail (SRE p.193)
Exception: expensive catchup operation with checkpoints: check the deadline only after writing the checkpoint (SRE p.193)
Cancellation: hedged requests send the RPC to a primary and then to other instances; on receiving the first response cancel the others; propagate the cancellation through the whole stack (SRE p.193)

Queue under bursty traffic (p.189): size the queue by the current number of threads in use, by the processing time of each request and by the size and frequency of the bursts; steady traffic: small queue (50% of the pool or less); Gmail uses queueless servers with failover to other tasks (SRE p.189)
Rate limiting in reverse proxies, balancers and tasks; ignores global health and may not stop a failure already under way (SRE p.189)
Watchdog (note 108): a thread that wakes up periodically and kills the server if there has been no work since the last check (SRE p.200)
The '2x the average' rule for deadlines is not from the book: it only says the deadline should not be orders of magnitude above the average (SRE p.193-194)
Death spiral: GC death spiral and death spiral from lack of resources (cold cache, query of death) (SRE p.187-188, 194-196)

Recognizing a bad retry in an emergency: it may not be obvious; the retry rate graph can be read as a symptom and not as an aggravating cause; mitigation = special case of insufficient capacity: fix the retry (usually a code push), reduce the load or cut the requests (SRE p.192)

Restart servers when Java is in a GC death spiral, there are requests without a deadline consuming threads, or a deadlock, but only after identifying the origin of the cascade, as a canary and slowly, since it can amplify the cascade (cold cache) (SRE p.198)

Load shedding by count: HTTP 503 to the new request when more than N requests are in flight; LIFO or CoDel queue instead of FIFO discards what is not worth processing (example: RPC 10 s in the queue, user already reloaded), well combined with propagating deadlines (SRE p.189-190)

Graceful degradation = reduce the work by worsening the quality of the response (e.g. search only a cached subset, faster and less accurate ranking); it should not trigger often; a path that is never used does not work, so exercise it by running a subset of servers near overload; monitor and alert when too many servers enter the mode; be able to switch it off quickly; keeping this configuration in a consistent system such as Chubby speeds up deploy but creates the risk of synchronized failure (SRE p.190)

consenso.name: Distributed consensus
consenso.summary: Where there is leader election, shared state or locking, use consensus.
rules: CAP; ACID x BASE (SRE p.201-203)
Heartbeats/STONITH lead to split-brain (SRE p.203)
Quorum 2f+1; minimum 3; 5 to tolerate a failure during maintenance (SRE p.216)
Approaches smaller than consensus are a 'ticking bomb' (SRE p.224)
Replicas: 2f+1 tolerates f failures; minimum 3; 3 replicas tolerate 1 (planned maintenance is most of the downtime); 5 replicas to tolerate a failure during maintenance (SRE p.216)
5 replicas: quorum 3, 40% can be missing; 6 replicas: quorum 4, only 33%; an extra replica in the same datacenter as another can leave the quorum without redundancy (SRE p.218-219)
A 10 ms write limits consensus to ~100 operations/s; 5 ms => ~200 [derived]; batching and pipelining amortize (SRE p.216)
etcd, Zookeeper and Consul are only named (SRE p.205); see etcd-zookeeper-consul

Patterns: replicated datastore (consensus on the critical path), leader election (equivalent to consensus; throughput matters less), barriers (avoid a single point of failure), locks with renewable leases and timeout, queues with lease, atomic broadcast equivalent to consensus (SRE p.206-208)

Multi-Paxos: strong leader, one round trip to the quorum; phase 1 establishes the view; changing the proposer costs and can produce dueling proposers (livelock); elect the proposer with random backoff (SRE p.211)
Strong read: a read-only consensus operation, a read from the stable leader, or quorum leases (a read lease to a quorum, ack from all replicas on write) (SRE p.212)
Fast Paxos is not always faster; stable leaders have costs (latency, leader bandwidth, bad machine); pipelining + batching; disk: 1 to several ms per write (SRE p.213-215)

Placement of leaders and quorum: concentrating leaders unbalances the network; 5 replicas with a link on the east coast: losing the link makes the RTT about 50% higher; hierarchical quorum (9 in 3 groups) (SRE p.220-222)
Monitor: members and health, lagging replicas, existence of a leader, leader changes (view), consensus transaction number, proposals, throughput, latencies, durable log time (SRE p.222-223)
not_in_book: installation/flags/TLS of etcd, Zookeeper or Consul

cron-pipelines.name: Distributed cron and pipelines
cron-pipelines.summary: Cron with Paxos and a leader; periodic pipelines are fragile; continuous Workflow; Moire load pattern (also in continuous pipelines).
rules: Prefer skipping to duplicating a launch (SRE p.226)
Idempotence or queryable state for partial failures (SRE p.230)
A periodic pipeline is fragile: hanging chunk, thundering herd, Moire (SRE p.233-236)
If the problem is continuous, do not use a periodic pipeline (SRE p.240)

Cron: prefer skipping to duplicating (recovering from a skip is feasible because owners monitor; a duplicate such as a newsletter may be irreversible; payroll cannot be skipped; an idempotent GC can run several times) (SRE p.226)

Cron state lives in the service itself (small writes on a distributed FS are expensive; few dependencies) (SRE p.227-228); Paxos logs on local disk, snapshots (the most critical state) backed up on the distributed FS (SRE p.231)
Moire load pattern: pipelines that overlap on a shared resource (peak near 1.2 M in the example) (SRE p.236); Workflow (2003): Task Master, leases, unique names, server token (SRE p.238-240)
Periodic pipeline: 40 min minimum interval for a ~20 min job in the example; nothing is harder than a pipeline job with 10,000 buggy workers (SRE p.234-235)

Moire is a problem related to the thundering herd, which can go unnoticed when the latter is seen in isolation; it occurs when two or more pipelines run at the same time and their execution sequences sometimes overlap on a shared resource (SRE p.236)
Moire can occur even in continuous pipelines, although it is less common when the load arrives more uniformly; it is most evident in usage graphs of the shared resource (SRE p.236)
Server token: protects against a Task Master swapped at the same address or a load balancer in front of Task Masters; a direct database would require a long transaction on every read (SRE p.240)
Spanner keeps journals, Chubby elects the writer, clients find the Task Master through naming services; the local Workflow blocks if the reference task does not leave the global one (SRE p.240)

integridade-dados.name: Data integrity and backup
integridade-dados.summary: Defense in depth; recovery matters more than backup.
rules: Layers: soft deletion, backups/recovery, regular validation (SRE p.248)
Replication is not backup (SRE p.247)
24 types of failure (SRE p.246)
Test recovery continuously (SRE p.254)
Gmail 2011: 4-day unavailability and 'more'; 24 h as a starting point; restoring from tape (GTape) with the estimate met and 99%+ recovered before the deadline (SRE p.242, 254-255)

Google Music 2012: ~600 thousand tracks removed (21 thousand users); 436,223 on tape and ~161 thousand without backup; 1.5 PB in 5,475 restore jobs, 5,337 tapes; ~7 days; cause: race between 3 h stages (SRE p.255-258)
700 PB at 300 MB/s by one task = 8 decades (1T vs 1E); parallelize across N tasks (SRE p.251)
Deletion alert: alert when the global deletion rate (aggregated across all users) passes an extreme threshold (example: 10x the 95th percentile), not per user (note 133, SRE p.260)
Blobstore: APIs with offline backups by default, end-to-end checksums and tombstones (soft deletion), which saved clients several times (note 128, SRE p.259-260)
A snapshot is expensive: it competes for the same capacity and yields less copy-on-write the faster the data changes (note 129, SRE p.260)
Music: the first root-cause hypothesis was a red herring; tape team alerted at 16:34 (Pacific) on March 8; recovery a few weeks after DiRT (SRE p.256-257)

Layers without PITR (p.247): PITR (point-in-time recovery, 'time-travel' at Google) is 'a chimera' in 2016 [DATED]; many projects use layered backup: expensive local snapshots retained for a few days, taken a few hours apart, plus full and incremental copies every two days retained longer; trade PITR for layers if needed, but never be left with none; if you can have both, use both (SRE p.247)

Harder variants (p.246-247): low-grade corruption or deletion discovered weeks or months after the bug reached production; longer retention requires old snapshots and merging with the current state, which complicates the restore (SRE p.247-248)

lancamentos.name: Launches (LCE) and capacity planning
lancamentos.summary: LCE and checklist; gradual rollouts; intent-based capacity planning.
rules: LCE: audit, liaison, gatekeeper, education (SRE p.262)
Spikes up to 15x; keep 4 or 5 replicas when 3 are enough (SRE p.265)
Feature flags 1 to 10 percent (SRE p.268)
Intent-based planning: specify requirements, not implementation (SRE p.150-151)
Keyhole at Christmas 2011 received 25x the normal peak (> 1 million req/s); 'make-children-cry switches' (SRE p.261)
Launch spikes of up to 15x the estimate; if 3 deployments serve the peak, keep 4 or 5 (SRE p.265); syncing every 60 s instead of 600 s = 10x the load (SRE p.269)
Auxon: small team + TPM, 2 years, initial 'Stupid Solver', agnostic allocation plan (SRE p.152-158); a new LCE trains for ~6 months; low-risk launch < 10% of traffic (SRE p.271)
Gradual canary on a few machines of a datacenter and the 6 requirements of feature flags (1 to 10 percent etc.): see topic canario-feature-flags (SRE p.268)
LCE is an SRE role and is encouraged to prioritize reliability; a company without Google's reliability goals, but with the same rate of change, may choose another incentive structure (SRE p.262)

When it pays off: fast-growing companies with a high rate of change, especially if they will double developers every 1-2 years and scale to hundreds of millions of users; LCE was Google's solution over about 10 years (SRE p.272)
One LCE drove 350 launches in 3.5 years and the team averaged five engineers: throughput of more than 1,500 launches in 3.5 years (SRE p.270)
not_in_book: SLO as a launch approval criterion

gestao-treinamento.name: Training, interrupts and embedding
gestao-treinamento.summary: Learning paths, interrupt management and recovery of overloaded teams.
rules: Weekly Wheel of Misfortune of 30-60 min (SRE p.280-281)
Polarize time (SRE p.287)
Embed an SRE: focus on practices, start with an SLO (SRE p.290-292)
A 20-min interruption = 2 context switches, 'a couple of hours' lost; polarize time; do not distribute tickets randomly (SRE p.287)
Embedding: one SRE; start with an SLO; kindling; Bad Apple Theory; postvitam (SRE p.290-294)
Joining the on-call as a rite of passage to celebrate; final exam or learning checklist; regular learning series on stack changes, recorded (SRE p.283)

Note 139: follow the RPC also applies to batch/pipeline (start from the operation that triggers the system); notes 147 and 149: the bigger side talks over the smaller; Conway's law (SRE p.283, 303-304)

engajamento-prr.name: Engagement model and PRR
engajamento-prr.summary: Simple PRR, Early Engagement and Frameworks/SRE Platform.
rules: Simple PRR in 6 phases (SRE p.308-309)
Early Engagement from Design (SRE p.310-311)
Frameworks reduce onboarding to one SRE in a quarter (SRE p.313-314)
Simple PRR in 6 phases: Engagement (1-3 SREs), Analysis (own checklist), Improvements and Refactoring, Training, Onboarding, Continuous Improvement (SRE p.308-309)

Early Engagement: SRE enters in Design, Build, Launch (dark launch = part of the real traffic goes to the new service and the responses are discarded) and Post-launch; disengaging is a positive result (SRE p.310-311)
Onboarding by the old model: 2-3 SREs for 2-3 quarters; with frameworks (Java, C++, Go) an idea reaches SRE production quality in days (SRE p.311-313; 'one framework per environment' is on p.312)
Shakespeare example: the PRR found dashboards that did not cover SLO metrics; the SRE took over the pager with two developers still in the rotation (SRE p.309-310)

PRR objectives: verify that the service meets the production setup and operational readiness standards and that the owners are ready to work with SRE; improve reliability in production and minimize the number and severity of incidents (SRE p.308)
Three models: Simple PRR (usually an already launched service), Early Engagement and Frameworks and SRE Platform (SRE p.308)

Analysis phase checklist: service-specific; the book only gives examples (do updates hit a large part of the system at once? right instance of the dependency, without using a batch system for end users? network QoS? errors in central logging? user-visible failures instrumented and alerting?) (SRE p.308)

Limitations of Simple PRR: communication overhead, the right SRE reviewers available, SRE work visible and reviewed by devs; the main one: engagement starts late, with the service already at scale (SRE p.310)

Early Engagement candidates: significant new functionality in a system already run by SRE; significant rewrite of an existing system; a dev team that asked for advice or a takeover at launch. SRE takes part in Design and takes over during or after Build (SRE p.310)

'One framework per environment (Java, C++, Go)' is on p.312 (not p.313-314); principles: codified practices, reusable solutions, common platform and control surface, smarter automation; instrumentation/metrics modules, request logging and traffic/load control (SRE p.312-313)

Framework definition (p.313): a prescriptive implementation for using a set of components and a canonical way of combining them; examples: standard monitoring dimensions, standard request log format, standard load shedding configuration format, consistent capacity/overload measure; C++ and Java implementations do not share code but expose the same API, behavior, configuration and controls (SRE p.313)

Shared responsibility (p.314): the original model had only full SRE support or almost none; in the new one, SRE takes load shedding, overload, automation, traffic management, logging and platform monitoring, and the devs do the functional on-call (application code bugs); typical onboarding by one SRE in a quarter (SRE p.313-314)
not_in_book: the complete checklist of a specific SRE team (the book only gives examples, p.308)

outras-industrias.name: Lessons from other industries
outras-industrias.summary: Four themes: preparation, postmortem, automation, rational decision.
rules: Themes of Ch. 33 (SRE p.316)
CAPA and near misses (SRE p.319-320)
HiPPO (SRE p.321)
UK nuclear industry: if the response must occur in < 30 min, it must be automated (rule of thumb) (SRE p.321)
Knight Capital: US$ 440 million in a few hours (2012); Flash Crash of 2010: trillions in 30 min (SRE p.321)
Nuclear navy: real drills 2-3 days a week; defense: 1 year of design and 3 weeks of code; Alcoa: report injuries within 24 h (SRE p.318-320)

Defense: a year of design followed by three weeks of code; very different from Google's launch and iterate culture, which promotes a faster pace of change with calculated risk; other industries have very different pressures, risk appetite and requirements (SRE p.319)

CAPA (corrective and preventative action) = systematic investigation of root causes; matches the blameless postmortem culture: assesses what happened, the effectiveness of the response, what would be done differently and the actions to prevent a repeat, without pointing at individuals; postmortems published among the SRE teams (SRE p.319)

Near misses are scrutinized like a preventive postmortem; CHIRP (UK) collects confidential reports from aviation and the maritime area; Alcoa: the CEO demanded notice within 24 h of a lost-time injury (SRE p.320)

Strategies: focus on safety, attention to detail, swing capacity, simulations and drills, training and certification (lifeguards), detailed requirements and design, defense in depth; SIL levels 1-4 in nuclear, military aircraft and railway signaling (SRE p.317-319)
Decision: nuclear 'if it works, don't change it'; 'the binder' of checklists; trading separates an enforcement team that switches the system off and on; see also HiPPO (SRE p.321-322)
'The binder': playbooks and checklists with every conceivable scenario in slowly evolving industries (SRE p.322)

incidente-shakespeare-ap-d.name: Incident #465 Shakespeare Sonnet++ (App. C and D): full narrative
incidente-shakespeare-ap-d.summary: Cascade of 10/21/2015: traffic 88x, sacrificial cluster USA-2, 2x failed due to an order-of-magnitude error, 10x, return 1/10/30/50/100%, outage 66 min, incident 89 min.
rules: Summary: Shakespeare Search was down for 66 min due to interest in a new sonnet; estimated impact of 1.21 billion lost queries, no revenue impact (SRE p.334)

Root cause: cascade from exceptional load + file descriptor leak when the search failed for a term outside the corpus; the new sonnet contained a word never seen in Shakespeare and it was the searched term; trigger = latent bug + sudden traffic increase (SRE p.334-335)
14:53 traffic +88x (post on /r/shakespeare); 14:54 OUTAGE begins; 15:01 INCIDENT begins (incident #465, IC jennifer); 15:18 file descriptor leak found in the logs (SRE p.335)

15:23 all traffic to USA-2 (sacrificial cluster) to allow increasing instances in the others; 15:28 2x increase; 15:33 tasks of the non-sacrificial clusters fail again; 15:34 order-of-magnitude error in the whiteboard math; 15:36 outage mitigated, new 5x increase (total 10x) (SRE p.335)
Traffic return: 15:41 1%, 15:45 10%, 15:50 30%, 15:55 50%, 16:00 100% (OUTAGE ends); 16:30 INCIDENT ends on reaching the exit criterion of 30 min of nominal performance (SRE p.335)
Calculations [derived]: outage 14:54-16:00 = 66 min; incident 15:01-16:30 = 89 min; declared 7 min after the start of the outage

Lessons: what went well was the fast alert (~100% HTTP 500) and the distribution of the new corpus; what went badly was being unpracticed in cascades and exceeding the error budget by several orders of magnitude; luck: a mailing list of enthusiasts with the sonnet, stack traces pointing to file descriptors, query of death solved with the new index (SRE p.334-335)

Example actions: cascade playbook, flux capacitor, cascade test in the next DiRT, plug the leak, load shedding, regression tests for queries of death, freeze production until 11/20/2015 because of the error budget (SRE p.334)

App. C (incident state document): IC jennifer, Ops docbrown, command post #shakespeare, exit = sonnet in the corpus + 99.99% availability and p99 < 100 ms for 30+ min; App. C marks 15:21 and App. D 15:23 for the diversion to USA-2 (SRE p.332-333, 335)
not_in_book: how many instances were the 'initial' capacity
the exact whiteboard calculation that was off by an order of magnitude

borgmon-dimensionamento.name: Borgmon: arena, 24 bytes per point, 12 h of horizon, TSDB and sum of rates (Ch. 10)
borgmon-dimensionamento.summary: Fixed memory block (arena) ~12 h; ~24 B per point => 1 million series x 12 h at 1 min < 17 GB; state archived in the TSDB; sum of rates defends against reset.
rules: Borgmon keeps the data in memory (checkpoint on disk) in a 'time-series arena': a fixed-size block with a GC that expires the oldest entries; horizon = interval between the newest and the oldest (SRE p.90)

Datacenter and global Borgmon are sized for about 12 hours of data (much less in the low-level collectors); ~24 bytes per point: 1 million unique series for 12 h at 1 min intervals fit in < 17 GB of RAM (SRE p.90-91)
Calculation [derived]: 1,000,000 x 720 points x 24 B = 17.28e9 B = 16.1 GiB (the book's '17 GB' works out if GB = GiB); 2.5 million series x 1,440 x 24 B = 86.4e9 B
'12 hours' is a 'magic number' (note 50): enough information to debug an incident in RAM, with fast queries, without costing too much RAM (SRE p.90, 98)
The in-memory state is periodically archived to the TSDB (Time-Series Database); querying old data there is slower, but the TSDB is cheaper and larger than Borgmon's RAM (SRE p.91)
Note 52: summing the rates (per task) instead of taking the rate of the sum protects against counter reset or missing data (task restart, failed collection); note 53: rate() handles resets (SRE p.98)
Counters do not lose meaning between samplings, gauges can lose activity (SRE p.92); minimum rule duration = at least two evaluation cycles (SRE p.94-95)

Example p.93-95: per-task rates 1; 0.9; 1.1; 0; 1 => 4 req/s; 0.6 errors/s => ratio 0.15; threshold of 1% and 1 error/s: the ratio passes, errors/s does not => alert not active; 'for 2m' (SRE p.93-95)
Topology: one Borgmon per cluster and a pair at the global level; scrapers below the cluster in large services; streaming between Borgmons (SRE p.89, 95)

Scripts x common format (p.89): instead of running custom scripts to detect failures, Borgmon uses a common data exposure format (white-box); mass collection with low overhead that avoids the cost of subprocesses and of establishing network connections; the collected history feeds the alerts (SRE p.89)
Notes 43 and 44 (p.98): varz is pronounced 'var-zee' (pronounce); the plural of Borgmon is Borgmon, like 'sheep'; the spelling 'Borgmen' is wrong (SRE p.98)
not_in_book: overhead of labels and indexes beyond the 24 bytes per point

balanceamento-vip-gre.name: VIP: id mod N, consistent hashing, NAT, DSR and GRE encapsulation (Ch. 19)
balanceamento-vip-gre.summary: Least-loaded breaks with state; id mod N remaps almost everything when a backend is removed; consistent hashing; NAT x DSR x GRE (current solution, 24 B).
rules: Least-loaded in the balancer requires tracking connections (stateful protocols); stateless alternative: id(packet) mod N (SRE p.161)
If a backend leaves, N becomes N-1 and almost all packets map to another backend; without shared state between backends this resets almost all connections (SRE p.161-162)
Consistent hashing (1997) keeps the mapping stable; Google uses simple connection tracking and resorts to consistent hashing under pressure (e.g. DoS) (SRE p.162)

NAT requires a per-connection entry and prevents stateless fallback; layer 2 (MAC) allows DSR (direct response, good for small requests and large responses) but requires the same broadcast domain, which Google outgrew (SRE p.162)
Current solution (2016): GRE encapsulation; balancer and backend do not need to be on the same network, 'even on different continents' (SRE p.162) [DATED]
Cost of GRE: 24 bytes of overhead (IPv4+GRE) can exceed the MTU and require fragmentation; mitigation: larger MTU inside the datacenter (SRE p.162)
DNS: the response fits in 512 bytes (RFC 1035); resolvers hide the client (EDNS0 is a partial solution); low TTL limits propagation (SRE p.160-162)

round-robin-least-loaded-wrr.name: Round Robin, Least-Loaded, WRR and subsetting: numbers (Ch. 20)
round-robin-least-loaded-wrr.summary: Round Robin up to 2x CPU spread; Least-Loaded has 2 limitations and ends up 'as bad as' RR; WRR reduced the spread; deterministic subsetting.
rules: Simple Round Robin: for years the most common policy; can give a spread of up to 2x in CPU consumption between the least and the most loaded task (SRE p.170-171)
Causes: small subsetting, variable query cost (the most expensive 1,000x or more the cheap ones), machine diversity (GCU), antagonistic neighbors (up to 20%) and restarts (SRE p.171-172)
Least-Loaded RR: uses the client's own count of active requests; the sinkholing trap (a sick backend responds with a quick error) fixed by counting recent errors as active requests (SRE p.172-173)

Two limitations of Least-Loaded: (1) the count of active requests may be a poor proxy for capacity (requests wait on the network; a machine 2x faster with the same latency); (2) the client only sees its own requests (SRE p.173)
In practice, in large services with Least-Loaded the most loaded task uses twice the CPU of the least loaded, 'performing about as poorly as Round Robin' (SRE p.173)

Weighted Round Robin: the backend reports query/error rates and utilization (CPU) in each response; clients adjust scores; drastically reduced the difference between the most and least utilized (SRE p.173-174)

Random subsetting (300 clients, 300 backends): subset of 30% => least loaded 63% and most loaded 121% of the average; 10% => 50% and 150%; deterministic subsetting leaves the difference at no more than 1 connection (SRE p.167-170)
Minimum service = 3 processes; typical 100-1,000; typical subset 20-100; flow control of 100 active requests; lame duck 10-150 s (SRE p.163-167)

decider-ads-mysql.name: Ads MySQL on Borg and the Decider (automatic failover)
decider-ads-mysql.summary: Manual failover of 30-90 min gave 99% in the best case; target < 30 s per failover; Decider (2009) < 30 s in 95%; -95% of toil; ~60% of the hardware freed.
rules: Context: Ads DB on MySQL; in late 2008 proof of concept on Borg; tasks move once or twice a week, tolerable for replicas and unacceptable for masters (SRE p.66-67)

Master failover took 30-90 minutes per instance; manual would give 99% uptime in the best case (below the requirement) and, for the error budget, each failover would need < 30 s, impossible for a human-dependent procedure (SRE p.67)
Decider (2009): planned and unplanned failovers in < 30 s in 95% of cases; from optimizing the absence of failover to accepting that failure is inevitable (SRE p.67)
Cost: all applications needed considerably more failure-handling logic; JDBC had to be customized (SRE p.67)
Results: time on operational tasks -95%; the loss of a database task stopped paging; with automated schema changes the total maintenance cost fell almost 95%; ~60% of the hardware freed (SRE p.67)
Calculation [derived]: 30-90 min => < 30 s is an improvement of 60x to 180x (1,800-5,400 s / 30 s)
not_in_book: specific financial cost of the Decider
aliases: automate yourself out of a job

knight-capital.name: Knight Capital: dead code under a flag and a loss of US$ 440 million
knight-capital.summary: The book cites Knight on p.83 (SEC order) and gives the amount on p.321: US$ 440 million in a few hours (2012); it does not give the duration in minutes.
rules: Ch. 9: commenting out the code or protecting it with an always-off flag instead of deleting it is a 'time bomb', as Knight Capital experienced; reference to the SEC order 'In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC' (SRE p.83)

Ch. 33: 'in 2012 Knight Capital Group found a software glitch that led to a loss of US$ 440 million in a few hours'; note 160 refers to the FACTS (B) section of the SEC order on the Power Peg software (SRE p.321-322)

In the same paragraph: the 2010 Flash Crash, attributed to a trader who manipulated the market by automated means, a loss of trillions in 30 minutes; 'speed can be negative if the tasks are badly configured' (SRE p.321)
The book does NOT give the duration in minutes: any '45 minutes' is [extrapolation]
not_in_book: duration of the incident in minutes
details beyond the cited SEC order

emergencias-cap-13.name: Emergencies of Ch. 13: Test-Induced, Change-Induced (config push) and Process-Induced
emergencias-cap-13.summary: Three cases, one lesson each: tested rollback (test), full canary + the luck of the push engineer (config), sanity check of an empty filter (Diskerase).
rules: Test-Induced: blocking 1 of 100 databases of a distributed MySQL took services down; the permissions rollback failed because it had never been tested; access restored within 1 h; the incident process was a few weeks old (SRE p.116-117)

Change-Induced: an anti-abuse infrastructure config pushed globally on a Friday caused a crash loop across the whole fleet; the push engineer rolled back within 5 min; incident declared within 10 min; some services took up to 1 h (SRE p.117-118)

Change-Induced, what was luck: the push engineer happened to be following real-time channels (not part of the process) and saw the complaints; the rate limit on full updates to new clients may have slowed the crash loop (SRE p.118)

Change-Induced, lesson: a previous push had a rigorous canary but did not exercise a rare keyword; the change did not look risky and had a less rigorous canary; conclusion: full canary regardless of perceived risk; noisy alerts got in the way (SRE p.118)

Process-Induced: two turndown requests in a row; an empty filter sent all the machines of small installations to Diskerase; traffic drained in 1 h; 1st installation rebuilt in 3 h; most of the capacity in 3 days (SRE p.119-120)

Process-Induced, cause: without a sanity check, the empty answer became an empty filter (zero means everything); slow reinstallation over TFTP at the lowest QoS and a regression of 2 setups per worker (SRE p.120)
'Tested rollback' is the lesson of the Test-Induced case (p.117); 'full canary' is from the Change-Induced (p.118): do not mix them up

etcd-zookeeper-consul.name: etcd, Zookeeper and Consul: consensus as a service (only named)
etcd-zookeeper-consul.summary: The book only NAMES etcd, Zookeeper and Consul as consensus services used by clients; Chubby fills a similar niche at Google.
rules: Many systems that use consensus successfully do so as clients of a service, such as Zookeeper, Consul and etcd; Zookeeper was the first open source one to gain traction for being easy to use; Chubby fills a similar niche at Google (SRE p.205)
Consensus as a service, rather than as a library, frees the application maintainer from deploying the system in a compatible way (number of replicas, group membership, performance) (SRE p.205)
not_in_book: installation, flags, TLS, authentication, tuning and operation of etcd/Zookeeper/Consul

bazel-blaze.name: Blaze/Bazel, hermetic build and Rapid/MPM/Sisyphus
bazel-blaze.summary: Blaze is Google's build tool, open-sourced as Bazel (note 37); dependency graphs; only the hermetic principle, not a migration plan.
rules: Blaze: Google's build tool (C++, Java, Python, Go, JavaScript); defines targets and dependencies; note 37 says it was open-sourced as Bazel (SRE p.78, 81)
Hermetic: insensitive to the libraries of the build machine; same revision => same result on different machines; fixing an old release = rebuild at the original revision + cherry picks (SRE p.77)
Ch. 17: Bazel builds dependency graphs, rebuilds only what depends on the changed file and runs only the tests of the changed code (SRE p.140; note 93 on p.147)
Rapid (releases, blueprints), MPM (versioned packages, dev/canary/production labels), Sisyphus (rollouts); Push on Green (SRE p.77-80)
No Maven to Bazel migration plan, no pom.xml nor BUILD/WORKSPACE files: only the hermetic principle and the mention of Bazel (SRE p.78, 81, 140, 147)

prodtest-turnup.name: Prodtest, cluster turnup and Diskerase (Ch. 7)
prodtest-turnup.summary: Prodtest = unit tests of real services + idempotent fixes every 15 min; turnup of 6+ weeks; Diskerase: empty set = everything.
rules: Prodtest: Python unit tests of real services per cluster, chained; it used to take 6 weeks or more from network-ready to live; mission: 5 clusters in 1 week (SRE p.68-70)
Each test paired with an idempotent fix that can run every 15 min; failures: latency between test and fix produces flaky tests; not every fix is idempotent (SRE p.70)
Triangle competence / latency / relevance; more than a thousand changes per day; Admin Servers (ACLs, RPC, review) instead of root SSH (SRE p.70-72)
Bigtable: automation assumed that 'first unused disk = machine without storage' and wiped the data (replicas saved it) (SRE p.68)
Diskerase: empty set interpreted as 'everything'; CDN wiped; only a latency increase; ~2 days of reinstallation and weeks of auditing with sanity checks and rate limiting (SRE p.74, 119-120)

dimensionamento-n2.name: Shakespeare sizing: 3,470 QPS, N+2 and regional distribution (Ch. 2)
dimensionamento-n2.summary: 100 QPS/task, peak 3,470 => 35 tasks; N+2 => 37; by region 17 US, 16 Europe, 6 Asia and 4 South America (N+1).
rules: Load test: ~100 QPS per task; expected peak 3,470 QPS => minimum 35 tasks; N+2 => 37 (an update takes out 1 task, a machine failure takes out another) (SRE p.35)
Regional peak: 1,430 QPS North America, 290 South America, 1,400 Europe/Africa, 350 Asia/Australia (sum 3,470) (SRE p.35)
With N+2 per region: 17 tasks in the US, 16 in Europe, 6 in Asia; 4 (instead of 5) in South America, trading N+2 for N+1 to save 20% of the hardware (SRE p.35)
Calculation [derived]: 17 + 4 + 16 + 6 = 43 regional tasks against 37 at a single site

comunicacao-colaboracao.name: Communication and collaboration (Ch. 31): Viceroy and the DFP -> F1 migration
comunicacao-colaboracao.summary: Weekly 30-60 min production meeting; Viceroy (2012-2014) united duplicated efforts; DFP: ~1,000 CPUs, 8 TB of RAM, 100 TB/day.
rules: Weekly production meeting of 30 to 60 minutes, rotating chair, standard agenda (SRE p.296-297)
Roles: tech lead, manager and project manager; the manager has two exclusive functions: performance management and being the catchall (SRE p.298)

Viceroy: dashboards; duplicated efforts for 12-18 months; project born in mid-2012; Consoles++ integrated in early 2014; completed at the end of 2014; general solution recommended for all of SRE (SRE p.298-300)

DFP MySQL -> F1: indexing system with ~1,000 CPUs and 8 TB of RAM indexing 100 TB per day; live migration with no impact, output validated against the old system; SRE and dev together from the start (SRE p.302-303)

Formal roles: tech lead (TL), manager (SRM) and project manager (PM/TPM/PgM). Well-defined roles: decisions within scope are fast and safe; fluid team (negotiated responsibilities): more mature and adaptable, at the cost of communicating more and more often. The TL answers for the technical direction; the manager has two responsibilities of their own: performance management and being the catchall (SRE p.298)

Specialization (one team per product): greater mastery and lower cognitive load, but silos and ignorance of the bigger picture; the aim is a clear charter of what the team supports and, more importantly, of what it does not support (SRE p.298)
Diversity: diverse teams are better (evidence cited in the book) and require attention to communication and to cognitive biases, which the book does not detail (SRE p.298)

fail-sanely-ap-b.name: Fail Sanely and best practices of Appendix B (empty DNS 2005, slash '/' 2009)
fail-sanely-ap-b.summary: Validate configuration inputs and, if implausible, continue in the previous state and alert; examples from 2005 (empty DNS) and 2009 (slash matched all URLs).
rules: Sanitize and validate configuration; faced with an implausible input continue in the previous state and alert; watch for empty, partial or truncated data (e.g. alert if the configuration becomes N% smaller) (SRE p.329)
2005: Google's global DNS system accepted an empty file due to permissions and served NXDOMAIN for 6 minutes; today it does sanity checks and carries on with the previous entries (SRE p.329)
2009: the list of suspect URLs became a single slash '/' that matched all URLs and the entire Web was flagged as malware; checking for a drastic size change would have avoided it (SRE p.329)
Non-emergency rollouts in stages, in different geographies and supervised; if something unexpected happens, roll back first and diagnose later (SRE p.329)
Measuring the SLO at the Gmail client took availability from ~99.0% to > 99.9% (SRE p.330)
Overload: reasonable but worse results, load shedding, tarpitting, a consistent subset of clients with errors; exponential backoff with jitter in every RPC client (SRE p.331)
SRE teams: <= 50% ops, 8 on call (6 per site), <= 2 events per 12 h shift; practice hypothetical outages (SRE p.331)

definicoes-cap6-p55.name: Definitions of Ch. 6 (p.55): root cause, push, alert (ticket, email, page), node and machine
definicoes-cap6-p55.summary: Ch. 6 defines the monitoring terms (p.55). Root cause (causa raiz) = a defect in a software or human system that, if repaired, gives confidence that the event will not recur in the same way; an incident can have several root causes and each one must be repaired. Push = any change to the running software of a service or to its configuration. Alert = a notification to a human, sent to a ticket queue, an email alias or a pager (tickets, email alerts and pages). Node and machine = a running kernel instance (physical server, VM or container). Dashboard, monitoring, white-box and black-box are also defined.
rules: Root cause: a defect in a software or human system that, if repaired, gives confidence that the event will not recur in the same way (SRE p.55)

An incident can have several root causes; example from the book: insufficient process automation + software that crashed on invalid input + insufficient testing of the script that generates the configuration; each factor can be a root cause on its own and each must be repaired (SRE p.55)
In that definition the software that crashed is one of the root causes; 'trigger' is a concept of the App. D template, not of this definition (SRE p.55, 334)
Push: any change to the running software of a service or to its configuration (SRE p.55)
Alert: a notification to be read by a human and pushed to a bug/ticket queue, email alias or pager; classified into tickets, email alerts and pages (SRE p.55)

Node and machine: interchangeable terms for a running kernel instance on a physical server, VM or container; several services can coexist, related (cache and web server) or not (code repository and Puppet/Chef master) (SRE p.55)

Monitoring: collecting, processing, aggregating and displaying quantitative data in real time; white-box: internal metrics (logs, JVM profiling interface, HTTP handler); black-box: external behavior as the user would see it; dashboard: summarized view of the core metrics (SRE p.55)
The book warns that there is no uniformly shared vocabulary, not even at Google: these are the most common interpretations (SRE p.55)
not_in_book: ITIL's or other frameworks' definition of root cause

reuniao-de-producao.name: Production meeting (Ch. 31): paging events, nonpaging events and the sample minutes (App. F)
reuniao-de-producao.summary: The production meeting (weekly, 30 to 60 minutes, with a rotating chair) is service-oriented and has a standard agenda: upcoming production changes, metrics, outages, paging events, nonpaging events and previous action items. Paging events: two questions (should it have paged the way it did? should it have paged at all?); if not, remove the non-actionable pages. Nonpaging events: three items (should have paged and did not: fix the monitoring so it pages; not pageable but requires attention: track it, including as reactive operational work; not pageable and needs no attention: remove the alert, which is noise). The sample minutes are in App. F (p.339). Portuguese terms: reuniao de producao; ata (minutes) in Apendice F (appendix F); agenda pre-preenchida (prefilled agenda); eventos que paginam (paging events) and eventos sem pagina (nonpaging events).
rules: Production meeting: weekly, 30 to 60 min, rotating chair (on the smaller side in a videoconference), service-oriented, not about people's status (SRE p.296)
Standard agenda (not prescriptive): upcoming production changes, metrics, outages, paging events, nonpaging events, previous action items (SRE p.296-297)

Paging events (tactical view of the pages): two implicit questions: 'should this alert have paged the way it did?' and 'should it have paged at all?'; if the answer to the latter is no, remove the non-actionable pages (SRE p.296)
Nonpaging events, item 1: something that probably should have paged and did not -> fix the monitoring so that it starts paging (SRE p.297)

Nonpaging events, item 2: something not pageable that requires attention (low-impact data corruption, slowness in a non-user-facing dimension) -> track it; this is also where reactive operational work is tracked (SRE p.297)
Nonpaging events, item 3: something not pageable and that requires no attention -> remove the alert, since it creates distracting noise (SRE p.297)
Previous action items: assign an owner and follow up; a catchall item; consistent delivery builds credibility (SRE p.297)
Mandatory attendance of the service's SRE team, stakeholders and development partners; agenda prefilled in a collaborative document (SRE p.297)

Sample minutes (App. F, p.339): outage #465 blew the error budget; 5 pages of AnnotationConsistencyTooEventual in the week, delay threshold raised from 60 s to 180 s (TODO martym); Nonpaging Events: None; push freeze for 1 month (SRE p.339)
p.339 is only the sample minutes; the handling by type of nonpaging event is on p.297 (SRE p.297, 339)
Sample minutes, Key Service Metrics: the book marks OK (p99 latency 88 ms < target of 100 ms) and BAD (availability 86.95% < target of 99.99%), both over trailing 30 days (SRE p.340)

Sample minutes, Resources: resources borrowed to respond to the sonnet++ incident, to be returned the following week; utilization 60% CPU, 75% RAM, 44% disk (before 40%, 70%, 40%); the action items go under New Action Items (SRE p.340)
not_in_book: maximum number of items per meeting

interrupts-tickets-scrub.name: Interrupts, tickets and scrub (Ch. 29, p.284-289): be on interrupts or don't be, give the pager back, policy
interrupts-tickets-scrub.summary: Three categories of operational load (pages, tickets, ongoing activities); a single engineer per shift; polarize time; ticket handoff. Regular scrub of tickets and pages: if the root cause is fixable in a reasonable time, silence the interruptions until the expected date of the fix (relieves whoever handles them and holds the fixer to the deadline). 'Be on interrupts, or don't be': whoever works tickets without being assigned distorts the measure of how manageable the queue is. Policy can be as powerful as code; give the pager back; requests should be meaningful, rational and bring information and prior work.
rules: Three categories: pages, tickets, ongoing operational activities; a single engineer per on-call shift (SRE p.284)
Polarize time; do not expect on-call and project work at the same time; do not assign tickets randomly to 'victims'; push manager; formalize the handoff (SRE p.285-288)
Be on interrupts, or don't be: working tickets outside your assignment ('to look busy') does not help and distorts the measure of how manageable the queue is; that is the book's reason (SRE p.288)
Actually analyze tickets: rotations become a 'gauntlet'; have a ticket handoff as there is for on-call; regular scrub of tickets and pages to find the root cause (SRE p.288)

If the root cause is fixable in a reasonable time, silence the interruptions until the expected date of the fix: relieves whoever handles them and creates 'deadline pressure' on whoever fixes it (SRE p.288)
The team sets the service level; it is ok to hand part of the effort back to customers; policy can be as powerful as code (SRE p.288)
Fragile and unimportant component: consider give the pager back, discontinuing or replacing it; time-consuming steps that do not require your privileges can go back to the requester (SRE p.288-289)
Guiding principle: the request should be meaningful, rational and bring the necessary information and prior work; in return the response should be helpful and timely (SRE p.289)
not_in_book: the book does not attribute the 'breaking of polarization' as the reason against working tickets outside the shift; the reason is distorting the measure of the queue (p.288)

canario-feature-flags.name: Gradual canary (a few machines of a datacenter) and feature flag frameworks: the 6 requirements (Ch. 27 and 17)
canario-feature-flags.summary: Almost every update at Google is gradual (p.268): the new server goes to a few machines of a datacenter, is observed, then goes to all the machines of the datacenter and then to the world; the first stages are the canaries; the installation tool rolls back automatically if the change does not pass validation. Feature flag frameworks meet 6 requirements: many changes in parallel, each for a few servers/users/entities/datacenters; gradual increase to a limited group, usually 1 to 10 percent; traffic directed by user, session, object or location; failure of the new path handled by design without affecting users; independent and immediate reversal of each change; measurement of the effect on the user experience.
rules: Canary of Ch. 27: new server on a few machines of a datacenter, observed for a defined period, then all the machines of the datacenter, then the world; the first stages are the canaries (SRE p.268)
The installation tool watches the newly started server and rolls back automatically if the change does not pass validation; it also applies to configuration files (SRE p.268)

The canary of Ch. 17 is another description: rule of thumb of 0.1% of traffic and increase by orders of magnitude every 24 h (note 89, p.147); the book does not fix a percentage of machines (SRE p.147, 268)
Feature flags, requirement 1: launch many changes in parallel, each for a few servers, users, entities or datacenters (SRE p.268)
Feature flags, requirement 2: gradually increase to a larger but limited group, usually between 1 and 10 percent (SRE p.268)
Feature flags, requirement 3: direct traffic to different servers according to users, sessions, objects and/or locations (SRE p.268)
Feature flags, requirement 4: automatically handle the failure of the new code paths, by design, without affecting users (SRE p.268)
Feature flags, requirement 5: revert each change independently and immediately in case of a bug or serious side effect (SRE p.268)
Feature flags, requirement 6: measure how much each change improves the user experience (SRE p.268)

Two classes of frameworks: interface changes and arbitrary server and business logic changes; the simplest for UI is an HTTP payload rewriter at the frontend, limited to a subset of cookies (SRE p.268)
Android apps: version offered to a subset of installs, percentage rises up to 100%; an invitation system is another gradual rollout (SRE p.268)
not_in_book: fixed percentage of machines for the canary
automated canary analysis under that name

shadow-on-call-cap28.name: Shadow on-call, reverse shadow and postmortem co-authorship (Ch. 28, p.281-283)
shadow-on-call-cap28.summary: Before shadowing, the student internalizes the on-call learning checklist; the alerting system copies the pages to the newcomer, at first only during business hours; the newcomer is not the on-caller (no time pressure) and follows the outage live; afterwards the on-caller reviews the reasoning with them; in the postmortem the newcomer joins as co-author; reverse shadow: the newcomer becomes primary and the experienced one observes without modifying state.
rules: Checklist before shadowing: the student must internalize the list before being eligible as a shadow on-caller (SRE p.281)
Copy the pages to the newcomer, at first only during business hours; the newcomer is not the designated on-caller, so there is no time pressure (SRE p.282)
Tip: include the newcomer as co-author of the postmortem, do not dump the writing on them alone, so it does not look like grunt work for the most junior (SRE p.282)
Reverse shadow: the newcomer is the primary and owns the escalations; the experienced one diagnoses independently without modifying state and helps if needed (SRE p.282)
Rite of passage: the apprentice joins the on-call when they reason through most of the stack and improvise on the rest; final exam or completed checklist; celebrate (SRE p.283)
Notes: 136 proactive (automation, design consulting, launch coordination) and 137 reactive (debugging, troubleshooting, on-call escalations) (SRE p.283)
not_in_book: 24 h a day from the first day
the newcomer writing the postmortem alone

interrupts-fatores-flow.name: Interrupts: factors, human cost and cognitive flow (Ch. 29, p.284-286)
interrupts-fatores-flow.summary: Five factors for deciding how to handle interrupts (SLO or response time, backlog, severity, frequency, people available); all aim at the shortest response time without considering the human cost. Flow state: being in the zone increases productivity and creativity and also applies to low-skill tasks; a disruptive interruption pulls you out of flow. Stress comes from the volume of pages or from treating on-call as an interruption; only full-time interrupts stop being an interruption, but the ideal balance between projects and interrupts varies from engineer to engineer.
rules: Factors: SLO/response time, backlog, severity, frequency, number of people available; all support the shortest response time without factoring in the human cost, which is hard to estimate (SRE p.285)

Flow state: maximize time in the zone; applies to low skill and low difficulty (repetitive game) or high skill and high difficulty; elements: clear goals, immediate feedback, control, time distortion (SRE p.285)
On-call stress: volume of pages or on-call treated as an interruption (project and on-call at the same time); with full-time interrupts they stop being interruptions (SRE p.286)
Balance between projects and interrupts: people are happier with balance, and the ideal varies by engineer, who may not even know what motivates them (SRE p.286)
Distractibility: the example of Fred; part of it is policy and assumptions about interrupts and ongoing responsibilities; the team can manage the response to interrupts (SRE p.286)
not_in_book: that flow only occurs in creative and difficult tasks
that everyone prefers the same balance

prodtest-dns-p70.name: Prodtest of DNS and idempotent fix (Ch. 7, p.68-71, Figures 7-1 and 7-2)
prodtest-dns-p70.summary: Figure 7-1: in the ProdTest of the DNS service a failing test aborts the chain of the following tests; Figure 7-2: a failed test results in running only one fix. If the DNS test was blocked by the cluster configuration done by the Machine Database team, when the cluster appeared in the database the DNS tests and fixes started to work; if TestDnsMonitoringConfigExists fails, FixDnsMonitoringCreateConfig runs, then TestDnsMonitoringConfigPushed and, if it fails, FixDnsMonitoringPushConfig; repeated failures make the automation stop and notify. Idempotent: the fix can run again without harm.
rules: A delay caused by another team's configuration becomes a bug to extend their Prodtest (SRE p.68); it is prevention, different from the blocking by DNS dependency (SRE p.70)
Each test paired with an idempotent fix, executable every 15 minutes without fear of damage (SRE p.70)
DNS example: a test blocked by the Machine Database starts working on its own when the cluster appears in the database (SRE p.70)
If a fix fails several times, the automation assumes failure, stops and notifies the user (SRE p.70)
Failures in retrospect: latency between test, fix and new test produces flaky tests; not every fix is naturally idempotent (SRE p.70)
not_in_book: that another team's delay aborts all the tests
that the fix runs only when the test fails

config-modelos-p80.name: Four configuration distribution models and the unified repository (Ch. 8, p.80, note 36)
config-modelos-p80.summary: All schemes keep the configuration in the main code repository and impose strict code review. (1) Mainline: simple and decouples binary and config, but produces skew between the repository and what runs. (2) Config and binary in the same MPM package: simplifies deploy, limits flexibility. (3) MPM configuration packages: hermetic principle, changes each package without a new binary build (first_folio to bad_quarto by cherry pick), the much_ado label installs both together. (4) External store (Chubby, Bigtable, source-based file system) for config that changes frequently or dynamically. Note 36: unified monolithic repository.
rules: All schemes: configuration in the main source code repository and a strict code review requirement; each project chooses the model case by case (SRE p.80)
Mainline: first method on Borg; advantage: binary and config releases decoupled and simplicity; disadvantage: skew between the version in the repository and the one running (SRE p.80)
Same MPM package: for few files or files that change every release; simplifies deploy but limits flexibility (SRE p.80)
Configuration packages: applies the hermetic principle; build ID reconstructs the config; changes the flag without a new binary build; much_ado label (SRE p.80)
External store: Chubby, Bigtable or a source-based file system, for config that changes frequently or while the binary runs (SRE p.80)

Note 36 (text on p.81, tied to the sentence on p.77 about identical builds at the same revision): Google uses a unified monolithic source code repository [Pot16]; consistent with the single repository of Ch. 2 (SRE p.33, 77, 81)
not_in_book: that the book calls any model an anti-pattern
that config without review is an anti-pattern in general terms (p.80 only requires strict code review)

producao-sem-supervisao-p144.name: Mostly unattended production, MTBF and release cadence (Ch. 17, p.143-144)
producao-sem-supervisao-p144.summary: So as not to scale the number of SREs linearly, production must run almost always unattended (mostly unattended) and be resilient to minor failures; when manual SRE intervention is necessary, the tool must be well tested, otherwise the intervention reduces confidence in the historical data and forces waiting for the monitoring analysis. More versions released to users make the MTBF worse, but reveal areas that call for more test coverage; annual releases have an MTBF of one year. Cadence segmented by reliability budget; noisy break-glass. Portuguese terms: producao sem supervisao (unattended).
rules: Production mostly unattended, resilient to minor failures; a poorly tested manual intervention tool reduces confidence in the historical data (SRE p.144)
Letting users experience more versions makes the MTBF worse, but lets you discover where test coverage is missing (SRE p.144)
Annual release: MTBF of one year, no matter how much testing (SRE p.143)
Reliability budget segmented by functionality or team; SRE has its own budget (SRE p.144)
Noisy break-glass (open a bug) that does not turn off the tests (SRE p.144)
Rollouts must be supervised (monitored), a different concept from unattended production (SRE p.329)
not_in_book: that more released versions increase the MTBF

disponibilidade-agregada-p328.name: Aggregate availability x outage duration (Ch. 3, p.38, and App. A, p.328)
disponibilidade-agregada-p328.summary: An aggregate unavailability metric (X% of the operations failed) is more useful than the duration of outages for partially available services (several replicas, only some down) and for services whose load varies over the day or week. The App. A table assumes no planned downtime. By time: uptime over uptime plus downtime; aggregate: successful requests over the total (yield).
rules: App. A, final note: an aggregate metric is more useful than duration for a partially available or variable-load service (SRE p.328)
Availability by time makes no sense for global services, which are almost always at least partially up; the request success rate, yield, is used (SRE p.38)
The duration table in App. A assumes no planned downtime (SRE p.326)

compensacao-oncall-p101.name: On-call compensation: time off or money with a cap (Ch. 11, p.100-101)
compensacao-oncall-p101.summary: Google offers time off in lieu (time-off-in-lieu) or cash payment, with a cap at some proportion of the total salary; the cap limits in practice how much on-call each person takes on, ensures an incentive to participate and promotes balanced distribution, avoiding burnout and lack of time for projects.
rules: Adequate compensation for out-of-hours support: time off in lieu or money, with a cap on the salary (SRE p.101)
Function of the cap: limit the amount of on-call per person, maintain the incentive and balance the distribution (SRE p.101)
Context: at least 50% engineering, at most 25% on-call, minimum of 8 SREs at one site and 6 per site at two (SRE p.100)
not_in_book: the percentage of salary used as the cap
labor rules on stand-by duty (CLT or others): refer to legal or HR

cap2-ambiente-producao.name: Ch. 2: production environment, RPC, protocol buffers and single repository (p.28-35)
cap2-ambiente-producao.summary: Machine = hardware, server = software; Borg allocates tasks and BNS names them; Jupiter 1.3 Pbps and B4 on the backbone; storage D, Colossus, Bigtable, Spanner. RPC via Stubby (gRPC is the open source version); protocol buffers are similar to Apache's Thrift and, compared to XML, 3 to 10 times smaller and 20 to 100 times faster. Single shared repository, except Android and Chrome; changes to another project go to the owner as a CL for review; all software is reviewed before being submitted.
rules: Protocol buffers: similar to Apache's Thrift; 3 to 10x smaller and 20 to 100x faster than XML, not JSON (SRE p.33)
Google's RPC = Stubby; open source version gRPC (note 11) (SRE p.32-33)
A single shared repository, except groups with open source repositories (Android and Chrome); CL sent to the owner for review; all software is reviewed before being submitted (SRE p.33)
Borg: bin packing with failure domains; BNS; kills the task that exceeds the requested resources (SRE p.29-30)
Note 13 (p.35): probability of two simultaneous task failures assumed negligible; single points of failure (top-of-rack switch, power) can invalidate it (SRE p.35)
not_in_book: that Google uses Apache Thrift for RPC
Kubernetes beyond note 10 (p.35), which presents it as a descendant of Borg, started in 2014

rollout-nota-89.name: Gradual rollout rule 0.1% -> 1% -> 10% -> 100% (Ch. 17, note 89, p.147) and savings without a percentage (Ch. 18)
rollout-nota-89.summary: Note 89 (p.147): default rule of thumb: start with 0.1% of traffic and increase by orders of magnitude every 24 hours varying the geographic location of the servers (day 2: 1%, day 3: 10%, day 4: 100%); App. B (p.329) says the size of the service and the risk profile inform the percentages. In Ch. 18 intent-based planning brings cost savings (economia) and less toil, with no percentage. Gradual rollout.
rules: Rule of thumb: 0.1% of traffic, then 1%, 10% and 100% every 24 hours, varying the geographic location (SRE p.147, note 89)
Percentages and intervals depend on the size and risk profile of the service (SRE p.329)
Intent-based planning: greater precision results in cost savings, with no percentage figure (SRE p.150); Auxon: time savings and less toil (SRE p.155)
Level 3 of the abstraction chain (N+2 per region) is where Google saw the best gains (SRE p.151)
not_in_book: savings percentage between level 1 and level 3
fixed percentage of machines for the Ch. 27 canary

parte3-hierarquia-intro.name: Introduction to Part III and the origin of the reliability hierarchy
parte3-hierarquia-intro.summary: The Service Reliability Hierarchy, analogous to Maslow's (Monitoring up to Product), had not been developed explicitly until SREs, such as Mikey Dickerson, helped the US government with healthcare.gov (late 2013 and early 2014).
rules: Origin: Google SREs at healthcare.gov needed to explain how to increase reliability; note 41 cites Dickerson (SRE p.85)
Monitoring: without it you fly blind (SRE p.85)
Incident Response: resolving is not necessarily fixing for good; reduce precision, switch off functions or divert traffic; avoid adrenaline-driven improvisation (SRE p.85-86)
Postmortem/RCA: alert and act only on new problems; blameless culture; outage tracker (SRE p.85-87)
Testing, Capacity Planning, Development and Product detailed in SRE p.87
not_in_book: numeric values or criteria per step of the hierarchy

notas-17-18-cap4.name: Notes 17 and 18 of Ch. 4 (p.50)
notas-17-18-cap4.summary: Note 17: if you never win a conversation about SLOs, it may not be worth having an SRE team; note 18: fault injection has another purpose but helps set expectations.
rules: Note 17 (SRE p.50; call-out on p.49): without winning conversations about SLOs, it is probably not worth having SRE for the product
Note 18 (SRE p.50; call-out on p.49, Don't overachieve): failure injection serves another purpose, but helps set expectations

config-linguagem-interpretada-p145.name: Config in an interpreted language and integration tests (p.145)
config-linguagem-interpretada-p145.summary: Loading config in an interpreted language (interpreted languages) is executing a program, with no upper bound on inefficiency; integration test with a deadline check; YAML with safe_load and protobuf give limited load.
rules: Config in an interpreted language is risky: loading = executing a program, with no upper bound on time (SRE p.145)
Test with a deadline check in all integration test methods; whatever does not finish counts as a failure (SRE p.145)
YAML with a tested parser (safe_load) gives a hard upper bound; a simple schema has no time limit; protobuf checks the schema on load (SRE p.145)
Defense in depth; /etc/passwd read halfway: report, do not remediate (SRE p.145)

senses: flow control / lame duck in datacenter load balancing (SRE p.164-166)
cognitive flow state in interrupts, Ch. 29 (SRE p.285-286); see topic interrupts-fatores-flow
shadow on-call and reverse shadow in training, Ch. 28 (SRE p.281-283); see topic shadow-on-call-cap28
shadow traffic is not a term of the book in this sense (dark launch appears in Ch. 32, p.310-311)
DNS balancing at the frontend (SRE p.160-162)
ProdTest of the DNS service and idempotent fixes in Ch. 7 (SRE p.68-71); see topic prodtest-dns-p70
empty DNS file in 2005 in App. B (SRE p.329)
configuration testing and cadence of config files in Ch. 17 (SRE p.138, 144-145)
four configuration distribution models in Ch. 8 (SRE p.80); see topic config-modelos-p80

QPS as SLI/SLO: the QPS of external requests is determined by users and no SLO is set for it; the book's SLO example uses average latency < 100 ms; QPS and latency can be linked (performance cliff) (SRE p.45)
QPS as a capacity/load measure: measure capacity in CPU and not in QPS (SRE p.175-176); breaking points and numeric cascade examples (SRE p.188-192)
